text:
Work flow


The normal work flow:

R script which contains the R code that produces,
Our R output: Figures and Tables,
An MS Word document, which is the report describing our results.



. . .
It’s disadvantages:

Every time the output changes, we have to revise the Word document.
If we comment our R code a lot (as is good practice), we have excessive #, and much will be repeated in the ‘Data and Methods’ section of the Word document.

\(\rightarrow\) R Markdown combines R and Markdown to overcome these limitations.

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
MS Word versus Markdown


Word is a so-called ‘What You See is What You Get’ text editor. That is, you edit your text and it looks just like the final formatted document.


. . .
Markdown separates text editing in source files, from the resulting formatted output. The source files contain your text and very simple formatting commands:
# This is a (level 1) header
This is just some plain text, maybe an introduction
to your final paper.

## This is a (level 2) sub-header
Again this is just some simple text. But in this text,
I also want to *emphasize* something. In fact, I want
to make it **bold**!

R Markdown


R Markdown allows you to insert R code chunks into your Markdown source file:
# This is a (level 1) header
This is just some plain text, maybe an introduction
to your final paper.

## This is a (level 2) sub-header
Again this is just some simple text. But in this text,
I also want to *emphasize* something. In fact, I want
to make it **bold**!

And this is some R code:

```r
mean(c(1, 2, 3, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
```

. . .
When you turn the source file into a formatted output, the R code will be evaluated and with its output, nicely rendered and inserted into your formatted document:

section: Do party positions predict how people think about immigration?
text:
Do party positions predict how people think about immigration?




But that would be wrong!

One of the critical OLS assumptions is the independence of errors, after all predictors \(x_{ij}\) have been taken into account:
\[\text{Cov}(\epsilon_{i}, \epsilon_{i'} | x_{ij}) = 0\] Breaching this assumptions does not bias \(\beta\) estimates. But it renders them less precise and statistical inference as overoptimistic (i.e., standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values will be too small, and t-values too large).

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Understanding the problem


In this simulated example, it is easily visible that the errors of respondents belonging to the same cluster \(j\) are correlated: \(\text{Cov}(\epsilon_{ij}, \epsilon_{i'j}|x_{ij}) \neq 0\). In consequence, the conventional OLS standard error will be too small, by a factor of:
\[\tau \simeq 1 + \rho_{x}\rho_{u}(\bar{N_{g}}-1),\] ::: {.note} where \(\rho_{u}\) is the within-cluster error correlation, \(\rho_{x}\) is the within-cluster correlation of predictor \(x\), and \(\bar{N_{g}}\) is the number of observations per cluster (Cameron and Miller 2015).
This means, statistical inference will be increasingly overoptimistic:
The more of remaining variation in \(y_{ij}\) (i.e., \(e_{ij}\) ) varies across clusters.
The less a predictor \(x_{ij}\) varies within clusters.

Consider our Manifesto variables: They are country-level characteristics and do not very-within out clusters at all; thus they should be badly affected.












:::

text:
Solving the problem The mixed model solution



Micro-level model

We start with a micro-level model, which acknowledges that the intercept varies by cluster:
\[Y_{ij} = \beta_{0 \color{red}{j}} + \beta_{1} x_{1ij} + R_{ij}.\] ::: {.note} - \(\beta_{0j}\) are cluster-differences in the average level of the outcome, adjusted for composition effects of the micro-level predictor(s) \(x_{1ij}\). - \(x_{1ij}\) is any micro-level predictor along with it’s slope coefficient \(\beta_{1}\). \(\beta_{1}\) has no subscript \(j\), which indicates that \(\beta_{1}\) is fixed across clusters. - \(R_{ij}\) are common random unexplained residuals, with \(R_{ij} = \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\).





Source: (Snijders and Bosker 2012, 45)


:::

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Mixed (random intercept) multilevel models



Micro-level model

We start with a micro-level model, which acknowledges that the intercept varies by cluster:
\[Y_{ij} = \beta_{0 \color{red}{j}} + \beta_{1} x_{1ij} + R_{ij}.\]

Macro-level model

We continue with a macro-level model that takes the varying intercepts as outcome variable:
\[\beta_{0 \color{red}{j}} = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1} z_{1j} + U_{j}.\] ::: {.note} - \(\gamma_{0}\) is the overall mean intercept. - \(z_{1j}\) is a macro-level predictor along with its slope coefficient \(\gamma_{01}\). - \(U_{j}\) are random unexplained group residuals, with \(U_{j} = \mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{0}^2)\). That is, the cluster-specific deviations from \(\gamma_{0}\).



:::

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Mixed (random intercept) multilevel models



Random intercept model

\[Y_{ij} = \underbrace{\gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} z_{1j} + \gamma_{10} x_{1ij}}_{\text{Fixed part}} + \underbrace{U_{0j} + R_{ij}}_{\text{Random part}}.\]

Fixed part: The slopes of explanatory micro- and macro-level variables and the overall intercept. These are non-varying point estimates and thus called “fixed.”
Random part: \(U_{0j}\) and \(R_{ij}\) are assumed to be normally-distributed random variables that are generated by unmeasured processes. They are leftover macro- and micro-level residuals. As random variables, their concrete values remain latent. We therefore only estimate their variances: \[\begin{align*}
\text{var}(U_{0j}|X) &= \tau_{0}^2 \text{ (leftover between-cluster variation)}, \\
\text{var}(R_{ij}|X) &= \sigma^2 \text{ (leftover within-cluster variation)}.\\
\end{align*}\]

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Further advanced topics

Beware that mixed (random intercept) models don’t work perfectly well if you have less than 30 clusters. Elff et al. (2020) discuss the problems in detail.
Interaction effects between a micro-level variable (e.g., education) and a macro-level characteristic are called cross-level interactions. They actually requite a more complex type of mixed (random intercept and slope model). Heisig and Schaeffer (2019) discuss these models and how to estimate them correctly in detail.

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Logistic mixed effects models
The upper-level equation is a simple linear model, but its outcome is \(\text{logit}(\alpha_{j})\)!
\[\begin{align*}
y_{ij} &= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_{0j} + \beta x_{ij})}}, \\
\beta_{0j} &= \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} z_{j} + U_{j}, \\
y_{ij} &= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} z_{j} + \gamma_{10} x_{ij} + U_{j})}}.
\end{align*}\]

text:
Linear probability model (LPM)


Using a linear model (and OLS estimation) to predict a binary outcome yields the so-called Linear Probability Model. LPMs predict the probability that the outcome equals 1 for each respondent \(\hat{\text{Pr}}(y_i = 1)\), given \(x_i\).


PlotCode






ggplot(data = ESS, 
       aes(y = (as.numeric(discr) - 1), 
           x = agea)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(size = pspwght), 
              alpha = 1/5, height = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(aes(weight = pspwght), 
              method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme(legend.position="none") +
  labs(y = "Probability of belonging to a group discriminated \n based on race, ethnicity, language, or religion",
       x = "Age") +
  theme_minimal()

Because errors of an LPM will always be heteroscedastic, we need to estimate robust standard errors.

Multiple predictors



# LPM with heteroscedasticity-robust inference
lpm2 <- lm_robust(
  formula = (as.numeric(discr) - 1) ~ 
    I(agea / 10) + I(eduyrs / 10)
  + gndr + cntry, 
  data = ESS, 
  weights = pspwght)

# Give a summary of both LPM models
screenreg(list(lpm, lpm2), include.ci = FALSE)

text:
The problem of linear models


LPMs may predict outcomes that make no sense! For instance, LPMs may predict probabilities larger than 1, or smaller than 0. \(\hat{\text{Pr}}(y_i = 1) > 1\), or \(\hat{\text{Pr}}(y_i = 0) < 0\).


PlotCode






ggplot(data = ESS, 
       aes(y = (as.numeric(discr) - 1), 
           x = agea)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(size = pspwght), 
              alpha = 1/5, height = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(aes(weight = pspwght), 
              method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              # draw line beyond observed cases.
              fullrange = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position="none") +
  labs(y = "Probability of belonging to a group discriminated \n based on race, ethnicity, language, or religion",
       x = "Age") +

This may happen particularly, when LPMs become complex (i.e., with many predictor variables). Note, if you only have categorical predictors, an LPM is perfectly valid and does not suffer from any problems (Angrist and Pischke 2009, Ch. 3.1.4)!






For old and low-educated men from Germany, our model predicts negative probabilities to belong to a group that is discriminated based on race, ethnicity, language or religion; what is that supposed to mean?!

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Generalized linear models (GLM)
The idea of generalized linear models is to stick to a linear model (i.e., \(\alpha + \beta x\)), but to map/project its results onto the range of the outcome \(y_{i}\).



We can achieve this by using so-called link functions \(g^{-1}\), along with their inverse \(g\):

\[\begin{align*}
y &= g^{-1}(\alpha + \beta x) \\
g(y) &= \alpha + \beta x.
\end{align*}\]

&= \frac{1}{1+e^{-(\alpha + \beta x)}}.
\end{align*}\]

We need a link function \(g^{-1}\) that maps/projects the results of our linear model to the range 0 to 1. One option is the sigmoid (i.e., s-shaped) logistic function, with its inverse the logit (logged odds):










Alternatives are the probit or cloglog link functions; results compared to logit hardly ever differ in meaningful ways.

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Logistic regression
Aka the logistic link function




Source: datacamp: Logistic Regression in R Tutorial




\[\text{logit}(y_{i}) = \alpha + \beta x\]

\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are now measured in logits (logged odds); difficult to interpret!
Re-transformed to probabilities, the size of \(\beta\) depends on the specific value of \(x\)!

Exponentiated \(\beta\) (i.e., \(e^{\beta}\) ) can be interpreted as odds ratios, or as multiplicative “effect” (i.e., a % increase).

text:
Logistic regression in R



# Estimate Generalzed Linear Model 
log_model <- glm(
  formula = discr ~ I(agea / 10) +
    I(eduyrs / 10) + gndr + cntry,
  data = ESS,
  family = binomial(link = "logit") # with logit link
)

# Give a summary of the LPM vs Logistic results.
screenreg(list(lpm2, log_model), include.ci = FALSE,
          custom.model.names = c("LPM", "Logistic"))

Remember, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are now predicting \(\text{logit}(\hat{y_{i}})\). Based on a regression table, we are left with interpreting direction and significance.

Coming up with a model of xenophobia means: Can xenophobia (i.e., \(y\)) be expressed as a function (i.e., \(f()\)) of another variable (i.e., \(x\))?

Now, the two critical questions have turned to:

What are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\)?

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Ordinary Least Squares


We find \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) by choosing the one line that minimizes the residual sum of squares:
\[\begin{align*}
      \min \text{RSS} &= \min \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_{i}^{2} \\
      &= \min \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_{i} - \hat{y_{i}} \\
      &= \min \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - (\alpha + \beta x_{i})^{2}
    \end{align*}\]

Note, how the residuals are defined only in terms of \(y\) and thereby differ fundamentally from those that PCA minimizes!

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
PCA
Intuition of the mechanics


According to PCA, it would be better to give imueclt a larger \(\beta\) than imbgeco.
The reason is that the respondents’ answers to imueclt are more varied. That is, one could argue that they contain more information!
Vice versa, variables that have mostly the same values across cases are not very informative. The key point here is: Cases are different — but variables with little variation make them look similar. PCA thus looks to emphasize variables with a lot of variation, to clarify how cases differ.

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
PCA
Intuition of the mechanics


Our measurement model \(y_i = \beta_{1}x_{1i} + \beta_{2}x_{2i} + ... + \beta_{k}x_{ki}\) projects the original data onto a new variable (i.e., in PCA lingo, a new coordinate-system axis, aka a principal component). But depending on how we choose the \(\beta\), many projections are possible; which one is the best?
PCA’s answer: Choose the \(\beta\) such that \(\text{Var}(y_i) \rightarrow \max\). That is, the new variable should vary as much as possible (i.e., should contain as much information as possible).



If you stare at this animation for some time, you will notice that “the maximum variance” and “the minimum error” are reached at the same time, namely when the line points to the magenta ticks […].


Source: “amoeba” on Stackexchange

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:

Intuition of the mechanics


Our measurement model \(y_i = \beta_{1}x_{1i} + \beta_{2}x_{2i} + ... + \beta_{k}x_{ki}\) projects the original data onto a new variable (i.e., in PCA lingo, a new coordinate-system axis, aka a principal component). But depending on how we choose the \(\beta\), many projections are possible; which one is the best?
PCA’s answer: Choose the \(\beta\) such that \(\text{Var}(y_i) \rightarrow \max\). That is, the new variable should vary as much as possible (i.e., should contain as much information as possible).



By the way, you can imagine that the black line is a solid rod and each red line is a spring. The energy of the spring is proportional to its squared length (this is known in physics as the Hooke’s law), so the rod will orient itself such as to minimize the sum of these squared distances.


Source: “amoeba” on Stackexchange

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Principal Components Analysis in R





A PCA produces components. You can think of them as the new variable(s), that is \(y_{i}\) of our measurement model.
PCA will produce \(k\) components, ordered by the amount of information/variation they capture. summary() tells you the importance of the single components. In our case, PC1 has a \(\text{SD}(\text{PC1}) =  3.465\), which is higher than that of any of the single items (e.g., \(\text{SD}(\text{imueclt}) = 2.4\) ). A component that captures less info than the most informative single variable of the original data is pretty useless.
The Rotation tells you the \(\beta\) for each component. \(y_i = 0.54x_{1i} + 0.63x_{2i} + 0.55x_{3i}\). Hence, you need to interpret the meaning of any component based on the \(\beta\)!

If you PCA items with differing scales (e.g., income, age, homophobia), you should always z-standardize! You do not want income to matter more if measured in DKK rather than Euro …
For PCA, z-standardization means that correlations between items become more important. That is, emphasis is given not to items that vary more (all have \(\text{SD} = 1\) now), but to items that correlate more with other items. This seems highly desirable!

PCA of xeno- and homophobia items — rotation needed


Because PCA tries to maximize the variance of each component iteratively/successively, the first component contains info from xenophobia and homophobia items. Conflating both types of items, which seem to measure two theoretically-distinct concepts, maximizes the variance on the first component. Therefore the PCA cannot clearly separate the two phenomena.
A rotation of the principal components that maximizes the distinctiveness with which the different items load on the principal components would solve that problem. Such a rotation could:

Conserve the orthogonality (i.e., uncorrelated) of the principal components: varimax()
Allow the principal components to be oblique (i.e., correlated): promax()

text:
Today’s general lessons

If we group data by several groups (e.g., countries and gender, or ethnicity and religion), we sometimes need to tidy/reshape data for our analyses. We might need to spread data (reshape from long to wide) into several columns.
Oftentimes we work with several data frames/tibbles. If they have some variables in common (e.g., time, place, type) they are relational data, because via that shared characteristic they are related. Relational data can me joined/merged via key variables. One-to-one joins are the easiest, but even one-to-many and many-to-many joins are possible. This means, for instance, you can join about every existing country information to your ESS data, or any party information to your Manifesto data.

Advantages of piping (and when not to pipe)

The advantages are:


Legible code: We can structure code from left to right, as apposed to from inside and out.
Shorter code: You minimize the need for local/intermediate variables.
Easily mutable code: You can easily add steps anywhere in the sequence of operations.



But:


If you have more than one or two major inputs, don’t pipe.
If you have more than ca. ten steps, better make intermediate objects.
It helps you to debug (i.e., find mistakes) and is simply easier to read.

Reminder (Standard errors & confidence intervals)


The standard error tells you the standard deviation of your result (i.e., mean, percentage, \(\beta\) etc.), if we would conduct the same study (i.e., the ESS) over and over again.
Standard error of the mean: \(\text{SE}(\bar{x}) = \frac{ \text{SD(x)}}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Standard error of a proportion: \(\text{SE}(p) = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\)
The 95% Confidence Interval tries to capture the range in which the true value lies with an accuracy of 95%.
\[\text{CI}_{95} = \bar{x} \pm \text{Critical Value} * \text{SE}(\bar{x})\] \[\text{CI}_{95} = p \pm \text{Critical Value} * \text{SE}(p)\]

Today’s general lessons

Data frames organize equally-sized vectors along their indices; Tibbles are modernized data frames. The indices of data frames/tibbles are organized as [row, column].
Helper functions are sub-functions that help you to make coding easier in many ways. They only work within the confines of the function for which they were designed as helpers.
Addressing variables means to address the columns of a data frame. Filtering cases means to address certain rows. Both is possible via the index [row, column], but the filter() and select() functions have advantages.
R has no labels. The idea is that numeric variables have a scale (e.g., cm, years, DKK), while categorical variables have no true representation in numbers. When you import labelled data from Stata or SPSS, the labels are stored in R but will create confusion in the mid run. Make sure to zap_labels() from numeric variables and to treat categorical variables as_factor().

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Factor vectors




Factors are for categorical variables that make a distinction but whose values cannot be compared on a common scale. They are composed of a sequence of categorical values (i.e., argument x), and a (ideally comprehensive) list of potential levels (i.e., theoretically-possible values).


conti
   Africa      Asia Australia    Europe N.America S.America 
        2         1         0         1         0         1

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Factors instead of labels






R forces you to decide whether a variable is continuous (numeric) or categorical (factor)



Numeric variables have a scale, such as cm, years, or DKK. Hence there is no need for labels.
Categorical variables, by contrast, have no actual representation in numbers.

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Recoding factors

Because factors are categorical, they cannot be numerically transformed. ::: {.note} What would be Africa devided by half in comparison to Europe devided by half?

If you nevertheless try to numerically transform a factor, the result is NA (i.e., “not available”).


[1] NA NA NA NA NA




In R factors need to be handled as fundamentally different from numeric!


:::


Base R is rather confusing when it comes to factors. We learn to use recode functions from the forcats package, which is part of the tidyverse.

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Wait, what’s a package?




A package is a collection of functions and their documentation (sometimes also data). Some packages are pre-installed as sub-packages of R’s Base package. In addition, there are, currently, +17,000 (user-written) packages on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). The tidyverse and its forcats package are such user-written packages.
You can install any of the +17,000 (user-written) packages using install.packages("name_of_the_package").
Please all install the tidyverse package now by typing: install.packages("tidyverse") into the console.

Do not add the install.packages() call to your R Scripts! You will need to install a package only once, and not every time you run your script. If you want to update, use update.packages().

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
The library


Because there are so many user-written packages, they oftentimes contain functions with conflicting names. To avoid conflicts, you need to specify for each R session, which packages you want to work with. You do that, by adding the packages to your current R session’s library.
It is good practice to add all packages to the library on the very top of an R script. Please all add the tidyverse to your library by writing the following as the very first line in your R script.
Some tidyverse functions conflict with Base R’s Stats package. ::: {.note} You can always address a function from a specific package by initiating it with package::function().



:::

title: Einführung in R und Quarto
text:
Today’s general lessons

The most fundamental data type in R is a (atomic) vector: a sequence/chain/series of information. Elements of a vector can be addressed via it’s index [i]. We can feed vectors into an index of another vector to address certain elements.
There are different classes of vectors: numeric, factor, date, character, and logical vectors. We can transform numeric vectors with arithmetic operators and a myriad of different functions. We can recode factor vectors with the fct_recode() function.
R has no labels. The idea is that numeric variables have a scale (e.g., cm, years, DKK), while categorical variables have no true representation in numbers.
R code may be nested, that is, you can write functions into functions. More on that later!
NA: is “Not Available” and thus the code for missing values in R. NaN are impossible numeric values.
There are no value lables in R. You will need to decide whether a variable is continuous or categorical.
R functions are contained in packages, which are bundles of functions along with their documentation. To avoid conflicts, you need to add the packages you will use in a certain R session to the library.

The layered grammar of graphics

Source: Wickham & Grolemund “R for Data Science” (Grolemund and Wickham 2017)

ggplot2 contains many geom functions, which put layers of different types of geometric objects (e.g., points, bars, lines) over a coordinate system.

All geom functions depend on the mapping argument. It is paired with aes(), which stands for “aestetic”. Aestetics are the visual properties of your plot.
The most important aestetics of any graph are the y-axis and the x-axis. Therefore, aes() depends on x and y, because these specify which variable to map to the y-axis and which one to map to the x-axis.
But of course, aestetics also means, among others, color, shape, size, and so on.

If we want experienced discrimination by country and distinguished by color, ggplot2 estimates separate bars and, by default, positions them on top of each other. The result is a so-called “Stacked bar chart”.

You can change the positioning with the position argument. For scatter plots, the default is "identity" (basically means: “leave as is”), or "jitter" (add random noise).

Alternatively you can use geom_jitter(), which has options width and height that allow you to control the amount of jittering in % of the respective y and x variables.
